Be sure to run the following code chunk before continuing with the assignment.  

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(stat1080r)
```

We are going to use the `toluca` dataset from the `stat1080r` package for this assignment. Run the following code to make that dataset available in your global environment. Moving the dataset to your global environment is not required; it just makes it easier to view.  

```{r}
toluca <- stat1080r::toluca
```

The dataset explores the average time (`hours`) required to manufacture a certain piece of refrigeration equipment at 25 different production plants. Each production plant has a different lot size (`size`), and the point of this assignment is to determine if there is a relationship between the size of the lot, and the time it takes to make the equipment. 

# Problem

Before attempting linear regression, we want to first confirm that the data appear to share a linear relationship. Create a scatterplot using `ggplot2` that plots lot size on the x-axis and hours on the y-axis. 

```{r}
ggplot(toluca, aes(x = size, y = hours)) +
  geom_point()
```

# Problem 

Comment briefly: Does linear regression appear to be appropriate in this case? Explain why or why not. 

*Yes, linear regression appears to be appropriate because the points appear to follow an approximately straight-line pattern.*

# Problem 

Assuming that linear regression is appropriate in this case, use the `lm()` function to create a model that uses lot size to predict hours. Use the summary function to see the model coefficients. 

```{r}
tlm <- lm(hours ~ size, data = toluca)

summary(tlm)
```

# Problem 

Based on the linear model summary, does it appear that the observed relationship between work hours and lot size is statistically significant? On what basis did you make your decision? 

*Yes, the relationship appears to be statistically significant. I make this choice based on the p-value for the slope coefficient associated with size, which is extremely small. The null hypothesis is "no relationship", and the p-value suggests that getting a slope coefficient of 3.57 would be nearly impossible if the claim of no relationship were true. Therefore, I reject the null hypothesis and conclude the two variables are related.*

# Problem 

What is the predicted number of hours for a lot size of 30? How about the predicted number of hours for a lot size of 100? Get both answers at the same time by creating a dataframe with the lot sizes of interest, and then feeding that dataframe and your linear model into the predict function. 

```{r}
tdf <- data.frame(size = c(30, 100))

predict(tlm, newdata = tdf)
```

# Problem 

What is the predicted number of hours for a lot size of 2? Why is this prediction not meaningful? 

```{r}
tdf_2 <- data.frame(size = c(2))

predict(tlm, newdata = tdf_2)
```

*This prediction is not meaningful because no observed lot size comes close to a value of 2. This lot size would likely be too small to even build facilities on. Linear model predictions only make sense in or near the range of observed values for the x-variable, and a lot size equal to 2 is much smaller than the observed lot sizes.*

# Problem 

Using the code for the previously created scatterplot, add a linear regression overlay on your plot using the model coefficients you calculated previously. You will do this using `geom_abline()` which will take two arguments (`intercept` and `slope`), which are the linear model coefficients from the regression model you calculated previously. For convenience, please feel free to round your coefficients to two decimal places when using the `geom_abline()` function. 

```{r}
ggplot(toluca, aes(x = size, y = hours)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(intercept = 62.37, slope = 3.57)
```
